case.title: The Still Canal (part 2)
case.hook: The Gazette is back with a new job for me: judge their Bright Ideas contest. Pelican Canal needs its water moving, with no power bill. Which idea can really work?

body: Pelican Canal is a dead end. Its water hardly moves, so on hot days it turns green and smelly.
Moving water picks up air at the surface, and fish need that air. Neighbors want to get the water moving without a power bill.

case.question: Which Bright Idea can really get Pelican Canal’s water moving, and what makes it work best?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: Wind can do work. A farm windmill uses moving air to pump water, with no wires at all.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 1: the drop race
clues.t: Air is real stuff. Moving air pushes on things, like the flat paper and the fan’s breeze.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: turn the valve
clues.t: A waterwheel turns only when water MOVES onto it. More moving water, faster wheel. A wheel can’t make its own energy.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: count the red blade
clues.t: Stronger wind, hitting the blades head-on, made the pinwheel spin the most.

solve.title: Which Bright Idea wins?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Entry 2, the waterwheel. The canal water will turn it.
options.why: Check Clue 3. A waterwheel needs MOVING water to push it. Pelican Canal’s water hardly moves.

options.t: Entry 1, the dock windmill, facing a strong, steady wind. Moving air pushes its blades, and the blades work the pump.
options.why: Case cracked! Moving air carries energy, and blades facing a strong wind spin fastest. Real ponds use windmill pumps just like this.

options.t: Entry 3, the magic fan. It makes its own energy.
options.why: Check Clue 3. No wheel or fan makes its own energy. Moving air or water has to push it.

options.t: None of them. Air is nothing, so wind can’t push a pump.
options.why: Check Clue 2. Air is real. The fan’s breeze pushed the paper right across.

opts.t: From the moving air pushing its blades.

droprace.title: The drop race
todo: Pick a pair.
Drag the 🏁 flag onto the one you think lands first (or tap it).
Press Let go! Drop all 3 pairs, then turn on the fan.

why.t: Falling things push through air. If air is real, it will push back.

droprace.model: a model: dropped from about 1 meter (3 feet)
droprace.predictQ: Which lands first? Drag the flag onto your pick, or tap it.
droprace.needPredict: Predict first: drag the flag onto your pick.

pairs.why: Same paper, same weight! The flat sheet pushes against lots of air, so the air pushes back up on it and slows it down.
The light, fluffy feather catches lots of air. The air pushes up on it, so it drifts down slowly.
Almost a tie! They are about the same size, so the air pushes on them about the same. Being heavy didn’t make the baseball much faster.

fan.label: Round 2: a fan blows across
fan.line: The moving air pushed the flat paper and the feather far to the side, but barely moved the rock. Air you can’t see did that!

droprace.q: What slowed the flat paper and pushed it sideways?

opts.t: Air. It is real stuff, and moving air pushes.

opts.miss: Then why did the flat paper and the crumpled paper fall differently?
It was the SAME paper. What was different?

droprace.win: Air is real, and moving air pushes. Clue 2!

valve.title: Turn the valve
todo: Drag the red valve handle around, or press Open and Close.
Watch the waterwheel, the stone and the lamp.
Close the valve all the way and press “Spin by itself”.

why.t: A valve is a handle that lets more or less water through a pipe, like a faucet.

levels.note: No moving water. Nothing pushes the wheel.
A little moving water gives the paddles a small push.
More water hits the paddles, so the push is bigger.
Lots of moving water: the biggest push, the fastest wheel, the brightest lamp.

valve.handleLabel: Or drag the red valve handle around in a circle.
valve.spinNo: The wheel twitched and stopped. With no moving water, nothing pushes it. A wheel can’t make its own energy.
valve.spinYes: It is already spinning, because water is pushing it. Close the valve all the way, then try.
valve.q: Where does the lamp’s energy come from?

opts.t: From the moving water, passed through the wheel.

opts.miss: Did the wheel make anything when the water was off?

opts.t: The lamp makes it by itself.
opts.miss: Did the lamp glow when the valve was closed?

valve.win: No moving water, no energy. More moving water, faster wheel. Clue 3!

redblade.title: Count the red blade
todo: Run Test 1 just as it is set.
Then change ONE thing: the wind, or the way the pinwheel faces.
Press Start. Tap every time the red blade passes the top, for 10 seconds.

why.t: If you change two things at once, you can’t tell which one made the difference. Scientists call this a fair test.

redblade.tapBtn: 👆 Tap! Red blade at the top
redblade.readyLine: Go! Tap every time the RED blade passes the top.
redblade.countLine: You counted {n} spins (the model counted {m}). It goes in your table.
redblade.recount: You counted {n}, but the model counted {m}. Try again, and watch only the red blade at the top.
redblade.firstLine: Test 1 is the starting test: gentle wind, head-on. I set it for you. Press Start again.
redblade.notFair: Not fair! You changed TWO things from Test 1. Change only ONE.
redblade.sameAs: That’s the same as Test 1. Change ONE thing: the wind or the way it faces.
redblade.q: What made the pinwheel spin the fastest?

opts.t: Strong wind hitting the blades head-on.
Wind hitting it from the side.
opts.miss: Look at your table. Which test had the most spins?
What happened when the wind was gentle? Did it still spin the same?

redblade.win: Stronger wind, facing the blades, means a bigger push and faster spins. Clue 4!

zero.title: How many wind farms?
todo: Make your guess with the slider.
Read why.
Then tap each number on the real dam photo.
zero.guessQ: Florida has ocean on three sides. How many wind farms (big groups of wind turbines that make electricity) does it have?

reasons.t: Most days, Florida’s wind is gentle. Big turbines need strong wind almost all the time.
Florida’s strongest winds come in hurricanes. Those come only once in a while, and they are too wild for turbines.
So Florida makes more and more of its electricity from sunlight instead.
Florida DOES use moving water: one dam on the Apalachicola River makes electricity. Look!

zero.photoHead: The Jim Woodruff Dam, on the Apalachicola River at the Florida–Georgia line. Tap each number.
zero.alt: An airplane view of a long concrete dam across a wide blue lake, with a powerhouse building on the right and the river below.
zero.credit: Jim Woodruff Lock and Dam: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

spots.label: Lake Seminole
spots.t: The dam holds the river back, so this lake sits higher than the river below.

spots.label: The powerhouse
spots.t: Water rushes down through big pipes inside. It pushes the blades of wheels called turbines, and they spin.

spots.label: Water out
spots.t: After it pushes the turbines, the water flows on down the Apalachicola River.

spots.label: The switchyard
spots.t: The spinning turbines turn generators. The electricity leaves here on power lines.

zero.win: Moving water pushes turbines, and Florida gets electricity. That’s water energy at work!

windribbon.title: The wind ribbon
todo: Drag the time slider (or press ◀ ▶) through one summer day on the dock.
Watch the ribbon and the windmill.
Then pick the best time to pump.

why.t: A ribbon on a pole points the way the wind blows. The stronger the wind, the straighter it stands out.

windribbon.model: a model of one summer day
windribbon.pumpNo: Too gentle: this windmill needs about 7 mph to pump.

hours.label: 6 AM
hours.note: A light breeze drifts from the land out over the water. At night the land cooled off more than the water.

hours.label: 9 AM
hours.note: Almost still. The Sun is warming the land.

hours.label: 12 noon
hours.note: The sea breeze starts! The land is now warmer than the water.

hours.label: 3 PM
hours.note: The sea breeze is strongest. Warm air rises over the hot land, and cooler air from the water rushes in.

hours.label: 6 PM
hours.note: Still breezy, but the land is starting to cool.

windribbon.pickQ: When will the dock windmill pump the most water?

picks.miss: Check the ribbon at 6 AM. Is the wind strong enough?
Check 9 AM again. How many mph?
What happens to the breeze after sunset?

windribbon.q: Why is it windiest in the afternoon?

opts.t: The Sun heats the land faster than the water, so cooler air from the water rushes in.

opts.miss: Did the windmill spin when the air was still?
Read the 3 PM note again. What is the Sun doing?

windribbon.win: Florida’s afternoon sea breeze: the best time for the dock windmill!

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain how moving air or water does work, or what makes a wheel spin faster?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: Moving air and moving water push on blades, and a bigger push makes the wheel spin faster.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “moving air”, “moving water”, “bigger push” and “faster”. Those words hold the big idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
